questions.questionText:
Hypothesis Testing (Mean — Known Variance):
Bags of sugar are labelled 2.00 kg with σ = 0.06 kg. A random sample of 36 bags has mean x̄ = 1.975 kg. Test at the 5% significance level (two-tailed, critical z = ±1.96) whether the packing machine is miscalibrated. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: H₀: μ = 2.00; H₁: μ ≠ 2.00 [1]. SE = 0.06/√36 = 0.01 [1]. z = (1.975 - 2.00)/0.01 = -2.50 [2]. Since |-2.50| > 1.96, reject H₀: significant evidence at 5% level that mean weight differs from 2.00 kg [1].

questions.questionText:
Student's t-Test (Small Sample, Unknown σ):
Five battery lifetimes (hours) are: 18, 21, 16, 20, 20. Test at the 5% level (one-tailed, df=4, t_crit = 2.132) if mean life μ exceeds 17 hours. [6 marks]

95% Confidence Interval for Population Mean & Proportion:
In a survey of 200 voters, 130 support a new policy. Construct an approximate 95% confidence interval (z = 1.96) for the true population proportion p. [4 marks]

Chi-Squared Test of Independence:
A 2×2 contingency table compares Study Method (Visual vs Audio) against Pass/Fail across 100 learners: Visual Pass 36, Visual Fail 14; Audio Pass 24, Audio Fail 26. Test for association at 5% significance (df = 1, χ²_crit = 3.841). [6 marks]
questions.explanation: H₀: Study method and exam result are independent [1]. Row totals 50, 50; Col totals 60, 40 -> Expected: E_Pass = 30, E_Fail = 20 in both rows [2]. χ² = (6²/30)+(6²/20)+(6²/30)+(6²/20) = 1.2+1.8+1.2+1.8 = 6.00 [2]. Since 6.00 > 3.841, reject H₀: significant association exists [1].

questions.questionText:
Goodness-of-Fit Chi-Squared (Poisson):
Accidents per week over 50 weeks were: 0 (20 weeks), 1 (18 weeks), 2 (9 weeks), ≥3 (3 weeks), total accidents = 46. Test fit to Po(0.92) at 5% level, explaining why last classes combine. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Expected freqs (50 × e^(-0.92) 0.92^k/k!): E(0)=19.93, E(1)=18.33, E(2)=8.43, E(≥3)=3.31 (last combined so E≥5 where needed; df = k - 1 - 1 = 2 since λ estimated) [3]. χ² ≈ 0.0002 + 0.006 + 0.038 + 0.029 = 0.073 << 5.991 -> do not reject H₀: Poisson fits well [3].

questions.questionText:
Linear Regression & Correlation:
For 6 observations: Σx = 30, Σy = 72, Σx² = 190, Σy² = 944, Σxy = 414.
(a) Compute Pearson's r. [3 marks]
(b) Find the least-squares regression line y on x and predict y at x = 7. [3 marks]

Type I & Type II Errors:
Define Type I error, Type II error, and Power of a statistical test, illustrating with a hypothesis test of H₀: p = 0.10 against H₁: p > 0.10 for X ~ B(20, p) with rejection region X ≥ 5. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Type I (α): rejecting H₀ when true = P(X ≥ 5 | p=0.10) = 0.0432 [2]. Type II (β): failing to reject H₀ when H₁ is true (e.g., if true p=0.25, β = P(X ≤ 4 | p=0.25) = 0.4148) [2]. Power = 1 - β = 0.5852 (probability of correctly detecting genuine effect) [2].

questions.questionText:
Testing Difference Between Two Population Means:
Sample A (n₁=40): x̄₁ = 78.2, s₁ = 6.0; Sample B (n₂=50): x̄₂ = 74.0, s₂ = 8.0. Test H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ vs H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ at 1% level (z_crit = ±2.576). [5 marks]

Hypothesis Test for Binomial Proportion:
A seed packet claims 80% germination. Out of 20 planted seeds, only 11 germinate. Perform a two-tailed test at 5% level (or compute p-value) to test the claim. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: H₀: p = 0.80, H₁: p ≠ 0.80 [1]. Under B(20, 0.80), P(X ≤ 11) = 0.00998 < 0.025 (2.5% upper/lower tail) [3]. Reject H₀: strong evidence germination rate is below 80% [1].

questions.questionText:
Hypothesis Test for Poisson Rate:
Road junction historically averages 4.0 accidents/month. After installing traffic lights, 1 accident occurs in the next month. Test at 5% level (one-tailed) whether lights reduced accidents. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: H₀: λ = 4.0, H₁: λ < 4.0 [1]. P(X ≤ 1 | Po(4.0)) = e⁻⁴(1 + 4) = 5 × 0.0183 = 0.0916 [2]. Since 0.0916 > 0.05, do not reject H₀ (insufficient evidence yet at 5%) [1].

questions.questionText:
Paired t-Test:
Six learners took a pre-test and post-test; score differences (Post - Pre) were: +5, +8, -1, +6, +9, +3. Test at 5% level (one-tailed, df=5, t_crit = 2.015) whether revision improved scores. [6 marks]

Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Non-Parametric Test:
Explain when to prefer the Wilcoxon signed-rank test over a paired t-test, and state the test statistic T calculation rule. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: Use Wilcoxon when paired differences are heavily skewed, ordinal, or contain extreme outliers violating normality needed for small-sample t-tests [2]. Rank |d_i| (ignoring 0s), attach signs back, and take T = min(ΣR⁺, ΣR⁻) comparing against critical table [2].

questions.questionText:
Residuals & Extrapolation Dangers in Regression:
In a linear regression y = 10 + 2.5x fitted over x ∈ [2, 12], explain (a) why predicting y at x = 40 is dangerous, and (b) how a residual plot detects non-linearity or heteroscedasticity. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: (a) x = 40 lies far outside observed data (extrapolation) where linear relationship may break down completely [2]. (b) Curved U/∩ patterns in residual (y - ŷ) plots expose non-linearity, while fanning spread reveals non-constant variance [2].

questions.questionText:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation (Conceptual & Applied):
For a sample x₁,...,xₙ from Po(λ), derive the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) λ̂ by differentiating the log-likelihood function. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: L(λ) = ∏ (e^(-λ) λ^(xᵢ) / xᵢ!) -> ln L(λ) = -nλ + (Σxᵢ) ln λ - Σ ln(xᵢ!) [2]. Differentiate: d(ln L)/dλ = -n + (Σxᵢ)/λ = 0 -> λ̂ = (Σxᵢ)/n = x̄ [2].

questions.questionText:
ANOVA Concepts / Comparing >2 Means:
Explain why performing multiple separate pairwise t-tests across 5 treatments inflates family-wise Type I error, and how One-Way ANOVA solves this using Within-Group vs Between-Group variance (F-ratio). [4 marks]
questions.explanation: 10 pairwise tests at α=0.05 inflate overall false-positive risk to ~40% [2]. ANOVA tests H₀: μ₁=...=μ₅ in one step via F = MS_Between / MS_Within [2].

questions.questionText:
Queueing / Poisson-Exponential Link:
Customers arrive at a bank teller as a Poisson process with mean 12 per hour. What distribution models inter-arrival waiting times T (in minutes), and what is P(T > 10 minutes)? [4 marks]
questions.explanation: Rate λ = 12/60 = 0.2 per minute; inter-arrival times follow Exponential Exp(0.2) [2]. P(T > 10) = e^(-0.2 × 10) = e⁻² = 0.1353 [2].

questions.questionText:
Quality Control Charts:
On an x̄ statistical process control chart (target μ = 500 g, σ = 12 g, sample size n = 9), calculate the 3σ upper and lower Action Limits and 2σ Warning Limits. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: SE = 12/√9 = 4.0 g. Warning limits = 500 ± 2(4) = 492 g and 508 g [2]. Action limits = 500 ± 3(4) = 488 g and 512 g [2].

questions.questionText:
Pooled Two-Sample t-Test:
Samples from two soil treatments: n₁ = 6, x̄₁ = 42, s₁² = 10; n₂ = 8, x̄₂ = 37, s₂² = 14. Calculate the pooled variance s_p² and t-statistic (df = 12). [4 marks]

Covariance & Correlation of Transformed Variables:
Given r(X, Y) = 0.80, explain the exact effect on r if U = 3X + 10 and V = -2Y + 5. [3 marks]
questions.explanation: Linear scaling preserves magnitude of correlation, while negative multiplier (-2) flips the sign: r(U, V) = -0.80 [3].

questions.questionText:
P-Value Interpretation:
A researcher obtains p-value = 0.031 for a one-tailed test. State the conclusion at (a) α = 5% and (b) α = 1%, and warn against interpreting p = 0.031 as "probability H₀ is true". [4 marks]
questions.explanation: (a) 0.031 < 0.05 -> reject H₀. (b) 0.031 > 0.01 -> fail to reject H₀ [2]. P-value is P(data this extreme OR more | H₀ true), NOT the probability that H₀ is true [2].
